selected_passages.text: A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem. selected_passages.title: News publisher files class action antitrust suit against Google, citing AI’s harms to their bottom line
selected_passages.text: A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. [raw:sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]

selected_passages.text: Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

selected_passages.text: More importantly, perhaps, is the suit’s tackling of how AI will impact publishers’ businesses. The problem was recently detailed in a report on Thursday by The Wall Street Journal, which led with a shocking statistic. Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

[sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
- Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C.
- The lawsuit alleges Google uses AI technologies like SGE and Bard to misappropriate publisher content and reduce traffic to news sites.
- Plaintiffs claim Google's actions violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act, seeking monetary and injunctive relief.
- Reports suggest publishers could lose 20-40% of website traffic when Google's AI products fully roll out.
- The case follows a recent agreement where Google pays Canadian media $73.5 million annually for content use.

A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. [sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
- Sam Bankman-Fried was the former CEO of FTX.
- The trial took place on the second day.
- Thane Rehn was the prosecutor for the government.
- Mark Cohen was one of Bankman-Fried's lawyers.
- Damian Williams is the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.
- Caroline Ellison was the CEO of Alameda Research.
- Alameda Research is a crypto hedge fund owned by Bankman-Fried.
- Jane Street is a high-frequency trading firm where Bankman-Fried started.
- Matt Huang is a former partner at Sequoia Capital.
- Marc-Antoine Julliard is a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London.
- Julliard invested in Bitcoin and Dogecoin on FTX.
- Julliard tried to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8.
- Adam Yedidia is a graduate of MIT.
- Yedidia was a close friend of Bankman-Fried in college.
- Yedidia worked as a trader at Alameda and a developer at FTX.
- Yedidia has legal immunity during his testimony.
- Bankman-Fried spent about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison.
- The prosecution's story lasted roughly 30 minutes.
- Tom Brady and Larry David are celebrities mentioned in the prosecution's account.
- Fortune magazine is cited as having written about Bankman-Fried as a 'crypto boy' genius.

[sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
- Prosecutors alleged Bankman-Fried stole customer funds to finance his lifestyle, political donations, and risky bets via Alameda Research.
- Defense attorneys argued Bankman-Fried acted in good faith, built successful businesses, and did not defraud anyone.
- Witnesses included a victim who lost nearly $100,000 and a former friend who admitted to writing code that may have contributed to the scheme.
- The trial featured high-profile attendees including Bankman-Fried's parents, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams, and venture capitalist Matt Huang.
- Bankman-Fried spent seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison before this trial, resulting in more prominent cheekbones.

[raw:sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
The key to his alleged scheme? Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund he also owned, argued Rehn. Using Caroline Ellison, his on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda, as a front, Bankman-Fried had “secret access” to customer money—both cash and crypto—the government claimed.

selected_passages.text: The second day of the Sam Bankman-Fried trial featured starkly contrasting opening statements where prosecutors painted him as a liar who stole billions for a lavish lifestyle, while his defense argued he was a good-faith startup founder who acted innovatively. The day concluded with the testimony of victim Marc-Antoine Julliard and former friend Adam Yedidia, who revealed his concerns about unwittingly contributing to the alleged crimes through code he wrote.

[raw:sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
The key to his alleged scheme? Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund he also owned, argued Rehn. Using Caroline Ellison, his on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda, as a front, Bankman-Fried had “secret access” to customer money—both cash and crypto—the government claimed.

[raw:sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
Alameda was not subterranean or shady. It was a successful hedge fund, he said. FTX was no Ponzi scheme. It was a “very innovative, successful company.” And the business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker, or financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

[sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
- Sam Bankman-Fried was the former CEO of FTX.
- The trial took place on the second day.
- Thane Rehn was the prosecutor for the government.
- Mark Cohen was one of Bankman-Fried's lawyers.
- Damian Williams is the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.
- Caroline Ellison was the CEO of Alameda Research.
- Alameda Research is a crypto hedge fund owned by Bankman-Fried.
- Jane Street is a high-frequency trading firm where Bankman-Fried started.
- Matt Huang is a former partner at Sequoia Capital.
- Marc-Antoine Julliard is a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London.
- Julliard invested in Bitcoin and Dogecoin on FTX.
- Julliard tried to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8.
- Adam Yedidia is a graduate of MIT.
- Yedidia was a close friend of Bankman-Fried in college.
- Yedidia worked as a trader at Alameda and a developer at FTX.
- Yedidia has legal immunity during his testimony.
- Bankman-Fried spent about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison.
- The prosecution's story lasted roughly 30 minutes.
- Tom Brady and Larry David are celebrities mentioned in the prosecution's account.
- Fortune magazine is cited as having written about Bankman-Fried as a 'crypto boy' genius.

selected_passages.text: Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

selected_passages.title: sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line
selected_passages.text:
- Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C.
- The lawsuit alleges Google uses AI technologies like SGE and Bard to misappropriate publisher content and reduce traffic to news sites.
- Plaintiffs claim Google's actions violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act, seeking monetary and injunctive relief.
- Reports suggest publishers could lose 20-40% of website traffic when Google's AI products fully roll out.
- The case follows a recent agreement where Google pays Canadian media $73.5 million annually for content use.

selected_passages.title: sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line
selected_passages.text: Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

SBF allegedly tried to buy off Trump: The TC team’s been trained on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of cryptocurrency exchange FTX. But fascinating details about SBF’s political dealings are emerging from a book by Michael Lewis, “Going Infinite,” that debuted on the first day of the trial, like SBF’s attempt to buy off Trump to get him to not run again for president.

[sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
- Prosecutors alleged Bankman-Fried stole customer funds to finance his lifestyle, political donations, and risky bets via Alameda Research.
- Defense attorneys argued Bankman-Fried acted in good faith, built successful businesses, and did not defraud anyone.
- Witnesses included a victim who lost nearly $100,000 and a former friend who admitted to writing code that may have contributed to the scheme.
- The trial featured high-profile attendees including Bankman-Fried's parents, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams, and venture capitalist Matt Huang.
- Bankman-Fried spent seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison before this trial, resulting in more prominent cheekbones.

- Julliard tried to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8.
- Adam Yedidia is a graduate of MIT.
- Yedidia was a close friend of Bankman-Fried in college.
- Yedidia worked as a trader at Alameda and a developer at FTX.
- Yedidia has legal immunity during his testimony.
- Bankman-Fried spent about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison.
- The prosecution's story lasted roughly 30 minutes.
- Tom Brady and Larry David are celebrities mentioned in the prosecution's account.
- Fortune magazine is cited as having written about Bankman-Fried as a 'crypto boy' genius.

selected_passages.text:
- Prosecutors alleged Bankman-Fried stole customer funds to finance his lifestyle, political donations, and risky bets via Alameda Research.
- Defense attorneys argued Bankman-Fried acted in good faith, built successful businesses, and did not defraud anyone.
- Witnesses included a victim who lost nearly $100,000 and a former friend who admitted to writing code that may have contributed to the scheme.
- The trial featured high-profile attendees including Bankman-Fried's parents, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams, and venture capitalist Matt Huang.
- Bankman-Fried spent seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison before this trial, resulting in more prominent cheekbones.

selected_passages.text: A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Who is Sam Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX? Is he a liar and a fraud? Or did he act in good faith, and like many a startup founder, fly too close to the sun?

[raw:sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
But Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, was no liar, according to Mark Cohen, one of his lawyers. “Sam didn’t defraud anyone,” he said early on in his opening statement.

[sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
- Sam Bankman-Fried was the former CEO of FTX.
- The trial took place on the second day.
- Thane Rehn was the prosecutor for the government.
- Mark Cohen was one of Bankman-Fried's lawyers.
- Damian Williams is the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.
- Caroline Ellison was the CEO of Alameda Research.
- Alameda Research is a crypto hedge fund owned by Bankman-Fried.
- Jane Street is a high-frequency trading firm where Bankman-Fried started.
- Matt Huang is a former partner at Sequoia Capital.
- Marc-Antoine Julliard is a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London.
- Julliard invested in Bitcoin and Dogecoin on FTX.
- Julliard tried to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8.
- Adam Yedidia is a graduate of MIT.
- Yedidia was a close friend of Bankman-Fried in college.
- Yedidia worked as a trader at Alameda and a developer at FTX.
- Yedidia has legal immunity during his testimony.
- Bankman-Fried spent about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison.
- The prosecution's story lasted roughly 30 minutes.
- Tom Brady and Larry David are celebrities mentioned in the prosecution's account.
- Fortune magazine is cited as having written about Bankman-Fried as a 'crypto boy' genius.

[sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
The second day of the Sam Bankman-Fried trial featured starkly contrasting opening statements where prosecutors painted him as a liar who stole billions for a lavish lifestyle, while his defense argued he was a good-faith startup founder who acted innovatively. The day concluded with the testimony of victim Marc-Antoine Julliard and former friend Adam Yedidia, who revealed his concerns about unwittingly contributing to the alleged crimes through code he wrote.

[entities/nov-8]
- From [[sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]]: The date when victim Julliard attempted to withdraw funds from FTX.

[sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
- Prosecutors alleged Bankman-Fried stole customer funds to finance his lifestyle, political donations, and risky bets via Alameda Research.
- Defense attorneys argued Bankman-Fried acted in good faith, built successful businesses, and did not defraud anyone.
- Witnesses included a victim who lost nearly $100,000 and a former friend who admitted to writing code that may have contributed to the scheme.
- The trial featured high-profile attendees including Bankman-Fried's parents, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams, and venture capitalist Matt Huang.
- Bankman-Fried spent seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison before this trial, resulting in more prominent cheekbones.

selected_passages.text: A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. [sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
The second day of the Sam Bankman-Fried trial featured starkly contrasting opening statements where prosecutors painted him as a liar who stole billions for a lavish lifestyle, while his defense argued he was a good-faith startup founder who acted innovatively. The day concluded with the testimony of victim Marc-Antoine Julliard and former friend Adam Yedidia, who revealed his concerns about unwittingly contributing to the alleged crimes through code he wrote.

[raw:sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
What the jury will see is a nerdy startup founder who acted in “good faith,” not the prosecution’s “cartoon of a villain.” (Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried’s allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury.)

[sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
- Prosecutors alleged Bankman-Fried stole customer funds to finance his lifestyle, political donations, and risky bets via Alameda Research.
- Defense attorneys argued Bankman-Fried acted in good faith, built successful businesses, and did not defraud anyone.
- Witnesses included a victim who lost nearly $100,000 and a former friend who admitted to writing code that may have contributed to the scheme.
- The trial featured high-profile attendees including Bankman-Fried's parents, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams, and venture capitalist Matt Huang.
- Bankman-Fried spent seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison before this trial, resulting in more prominent cheekbones.

[raw:sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
But “all of that, all of it, was built on lies,” Rehn declared to the jury. “Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be.” What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets.
